LEARNING PATH LESSON · MUSIC ROOM · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Melody — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches melody — the tune itself: the single line of notes your ear follows through any song, the part you hum in the bath and cannot put down.

What is this?

A melody is a line of notes played one after another: the tune. It climbs, steps, jumps and rests — a path your ear walks. When you "can’t get a song out of your head," the melody is the part stuck there.

What does it mean?

Melody is music’s storyline in sound: ONE line at a time, going somewhere. Harmony and beat are the landscape; the melody is the path walking through it. Following that path with the ear — or drawing it with the hand — is music’s core skill.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three melody ideas: the melody is ONE line of notes in order — the tune; it moves like a path — up-steps, down-steps, big jumps; and the body can draw it: hand hills for the highs, valleys for the lows — the melody painted in the air.

Why this matters

Melody-following is the listening skill every other lesson here depends on — and hand-drawing the tune gives the ear a body, which is why music teachers have been air-painting melodies forever.

What it teaches

Melodic contour tracking (up-down-jump), hand-body mapping of pitch, hum-along memory, and the tune-versus-accompaniment distinction.

Words to learn

melodytunenotespathclimbjumphum

Say this to your child

“"The melody is the TUNE — the line of notes your ear follows through the whole song! It climbs like a hill, steps down like stairs, sometimes jumps like a frog. And your hand can draw it in the air: high notes up here, low notes down there. When a song sticks in your head, the melody is the part stuck — the tune is the traveller!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is melody — the tune itself."
  2. The path: hum any simple tune and trace it in the air — up here, down there, a jump! The melody is a path the hand can walk.
  3. The stuck-song test: what is the song part you hum in the bath? THAT is the melody — the line the ear cannot put down.
  4. Contour games: "sing me a melody that climbs… now one that tumbles down the stairs… now one with a JUMP!" The hand draws, the voice follows.
  5. Play the follow games below and close: "one line, going somewhere."

Look closer at the picture

On this card the word "Melody" stands in big navy capitals inside the rounded frame, with a friendly illustration below — exactly as the tune’s path looks.

Ask your child

"What is a melody — one line or many? How does it move? What does your hand draw when the tune climbs?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "The tune! The part stuck in my head!" "Hills and stairs and frog-jumps!" or the air-painter: "My hand walks the melody!"

Out in the real world

Melodies live in every doorbell, ringtone and lullaby — and the air-drawing works on all of them: trace the ice-cream truck’s five notes in the air, hills and all. The ear learns the path; the hand remembers it.

Try it together

Air Painters: one player hums a simple tune while drawing it in the air — hills, stairs, jumps. Everyone else hums along and draws their own copy. Then reverse: the leader draws ONLY with the hand (no sound) — the players sing what the hand says! Contour becomes visible, singable, funny. Finish with the stuck-song share: everyone hums the tune stuck in THEIR head, hands painting. One line, going somewhere — every time.

Understanding check

Ask: "What is the melody? How does it move through the air? What is stuck in your head after a song?" The tune, hills-stairs-jumps, the melody — three answers and the path is walked.

Parent tips

Draw BIG — contour needs whole arms, not fingertips. And simple tunes win: three to five notes make the clearest paths and the proudest painters.

This lesson pairs with the Melody flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Music Room (Class 23).
